 Vehicle fire on U.S. 17 in Leland raises questions about 2023 Kia recall
 2 hours ago 
 Kamy Smelser , 
 LELAND, NC (WWAY) — A vehicle fire on U.S. 17 in Leland caused significant traffic backups Monday morning, and the vehicle involved may be among millions recalled over fire concerns.
 The cause of the fire remains under investigation, but WWAY has learned the vehicle was a 2012 Kia Sorento, a model included in a major recall issued in 2023.
 Brook Lindbert was getting breakfast at Panera Bread in Leland when he looked outside and saw flames coming from the SUV’s engine compartment.
 “It was a pretty serious fire, flames were all through the hood,” Lindbert said.
 Firefighters extinguished the flames, but the incident caused major traffic delays for morning commuters.
 Officials said the driver was alerted by another motorist after smoke began coming from the vehicle. The driver reported that flames were already visible when she pulled over.
 In 2023, more than 3.3 million Hyundai and Kia vehicles were recalled over concerns that they could catch fire while being driven or parked. The recall included certain 2011 through 2014 Kia Sorento models.
 According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the vehicles’ anti-lock braking system modules could develop internal brake fluid leaks, potentially causing electrical shorts and increasing the risk of engine compartment fires.
 “The vehicle’s anti-lock brake system module could leak brake fluid internally and cause an electrical short. An electrical short could result in significant overcurrent in the ABS module, increasing the risk of an engine compartment fire while driving or parked,” NHTSA stated.
 The recall prompted federal safety officials to advise affected vehicle owners to park outside and away from structures until repairs could be completed.
 Michael Brooks, executive director of the Center for Auto Safety, previously investigated the issue and identified 31 fires associated with the recall.
 “This isn’t a defect that only happens while you’re driving. It can happen after you’ve parked gone into your house,” Brooks said.
 Lorinda Hixon, who spoke with CBS News in Los Angeles following the recall announcement, described a similar experience involving her Kia.
 “A gentleman says get over, get over your car is on fire,” Hixon recalled.
 Photos showed extensive damage to the front of her vehicle.
 At the time of the recall, Kia reported being aware of one engine compartment fire, three fires involving the anti-lock braking system unit and six instances of melting components.
 While the 2012 Kia Sorento involved in Monday’s fire falls within the model years covered by the recall, officials have not determined whether the recall-related defect caused the fire or whether that specific vehicle had an outstanding recall.
 The cause remains under investigation.
 Vehicle owners can check for open safety recalls by entering their vehicle identification number (VIN) on the NHTSA recall lookup website .
